articles.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
articles.summary: YouTube-style UI over 6,454 videos sourced from 39,834 HN comments since 2007.https://hackertube.org/

top_comments: I think there is a massive opportunity for this kind of feed disaggregation. Used to be the recommender and indexing of content was hard, now I believe we can likely build our own according to our own preferences.Haiku/Sonnet (or even Jev) can do a lot of the filtering work to rank and extend an RSS feed list.I think this gives us an opportunity to fully cut the cord from eyeball merchants who want us to maximally engage and therefore polarize their content.The big remaining hook will be the social graph; I am interested to see how far the EU push for mandatory interoperability will go. Another angle I’d support would be mandatory pluggable standards for your own ranking algorithm, but it captures less of the win than full disaggregation.
One of the most upvoted posts of the year is a static scrape with a UI? I want old HN back…
Made a books version of this: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50326821PS: thank you karpathy, been binging videos on hackertube.org

articles.title: Show HN: HackerBooks – HackerTube, but for books mentioned on HN
articles.summary: Saw Karpathy's HackerTube and wanted the same thing for books. So I had Claude build one (Opus 5.5).It's ~16.5k books that at least two different HN commenters brought up, from 2007 till now. Each book links back to the comments that mentioned it. Data is downloadable from the about page.To be clear: Claude wrote almost all of it, including the data pipeline and the site. I mostly steered and made calls, bought the domain name, etc.It counts mentions, so it's not perfect (praising a book and trashing it both count). If your favourite book is missing or matched to the wrong thing, tell me.

top_comments: Love it! :)

A couple of missing ones (that I expected to have been mentioned, aren't there as far as I can tell, and I found them on here with a quick google):https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Invention_of_Morel mentioned here https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=28779266 I'd have expected it to come up as one step removed from Borges, and it did.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Why%27s_(poignant)_Guide_to_Ru... mentioned many times, eg https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36632010 - a surprising omission, tho I guess it's not in print.

articles.title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
articles.summary: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks

top_comments: IMO the largest true value of the frameworks (and languages to some extent) is how they help long-running projects with many people coming and going. The most valuable trait was not what framework allowed, but what framework disallowed, preventing foot guns. E.g. Java got popular because it forced everyone to code similarly, at least more similar than other languages at that time.But for agents it doesn't matter, so why frameworks at all?PS: authors comparison is not relevant, as it's simple mostly-static app with very little cross-dependencies, localizations, component re-usage.

The are some very real costs to JavaScript frameworks. These frameworks do not exist to empower developers. They exist to:* so that employers do not have to invest in training developers.* to ease candidate selection at hiring, which greases the wheels of hiring/firingIn the big corporate world, especially at non-software companies, there is a culture that strongly believes internally written software sucks. This is Invented Here syndrome, and it reflects that internal developers cannot write software and employers will not invest in maintenance.The larger costs there are human costs, the inability to efficiently solve any problem outside the constraints imposed by the framework.

> Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc.Yes, of course they asked.The agents responded with how this framework is X, not Y. How creating it was a sharp commentary on other frameworks. A couple honest caveats, and a succinct bottom line that adequately kissed the user's ass.

articles.title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
articles.summary: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it

top_comments: > To me, someone who chooses a worthwhile problem, obtains a proof completely using AI, understands it thoroughly, and uses it to develop interesting further questions or directions has made a substantial mathematical contribution. I would give that person substantial credit even if they supplied no new ingredient in the original proof.Yup. This is what Terence Tao has been saying about digestion of results for several months now. Mathematics has become a field where results themselves matter less, the social aspect of attracting others to understand your results and explore new problems has become more important.In a sense it is a little bit like software engineering, where writing code can sometimes be delegated to AI, and is arguably less important than understanding what the customer really wants from this software.

Isn't it the passage of mathematics from the age of craftsmanship to the age of industrial making ?My recent take on AI is that people haven't adapted to the new huge potential of the tool, and don't dream big enough (yet).It's like seeing a car engine for the first time, lamenting about the future of horses, and not realizing it'll also help us fly.

Why do nearly all the articles exploring the development of AI applied to math assume that capabilities won’t extend beyond theorem proving?> other skills will matter more: choosing which terrain is worth exploring, steering fleets of airplanes, and explaining what they find to the rest of the world.These all seem totally achievable by LLM agents, or at least, I don’t see an obvious reason why it wouldn’t be. 3blue1brown’s recent discussion on this subject was a bit better, but he spent the plurality of main body of the video assuming this scenario, devoting less time to the other possibilities. To me, it seems dangerous to build a math career on the foundation that AI won’t be able to explain math well in a few years, let alone a few months (which seems entirely plausible given the recent math progress).

articles.title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
articles.summary: I have been researching what the ultimate diff tool would look like, based on actual diffs in open source repositories.OmniDiff can diff: code (25 languages), config, images, PDFs, archives, cursors, fonts...It's fast. It can diff C++ files of tens of thousands of lines in under 100ms, on a 2023 ThinkPad T14s.It's open source. AGPLv3.It's based on real diffs. I looked at the 7400 repositories that are listed in Gentoo packages, sampled 2000 diffs and solved them manually to get a good understanding of what is needed, before putting together the diff pipelines for each content type. Incidentally, this also forms the basis of the CI pipeline, so the robustness of the codebase is quite high.I'm still developing it. It's v0.3.0 at this time. But I have been using it daily as my git difftool for months now, and it works well.AI Disclosure: Yes, I do use AI. No, I do not vibecode.

top_comments: Is there a way to use it with git without having to change your global git config? I.e. `git diff | omnidiff` or something?You can do this with delta: `git diff | delta --side-by-side`

cool to see fresh Rust software with copyleft license !I feel safer, as a user, enjoying the freedoms that the AGPL provides me. (No evil middleman will be able to give me non-free versions of this program.)

Nicely done OP. Does it do 3-way diffs for merges as well? The instructions only mention the two-way `git difftool` configuration so maybe that'll be a future feature?Any interest in getting the setup upstreamed[1] so that users only need to `git config --global diff.tool omnidiff` to enable it by default? Disclosure: I created `git difftool` a long time ago, and am always happy when builtin support for useful tools are added to it. Feel free to reach out if you'd like help making that happen.[1] https://github.com/git/git/tree/master/mergetools

articles.title: Ask HN: Which TV do you recommend for privacy?
articles.summary: I haven’t owned a TV in years and would like one that respects my privacy. Are there any TV’s which do this well? I am looking for something in the 60”to 80”range and would like a 4k display with at least 60hz display. I don’t mind paying a premium.I have heard good things about Apple TV as a better alternative to most smart TV native apps. Would some TV’s pair better with this than others for privacy? I don’t want the TV doing anything other than being the display for Apple TV.I am curious what success others have had.

top_comments: Recently I've had to deal with this same problem - get a new TV for living room. Personally, I do not watch TV at all, but kids want to see cartoons when having their breakfast. I spent a week reading forums and came to conclusion that best solution would be to buy a "dumb TV" and connect it to a PC I trust, but it appears there are no dump TVs in my rage of 55" and larger. So, I bought "Google TV" based TCL.When I brought it home, I never connected it to Ethernet or WiFi. Instead, I connected it to my laptop over USB, then using adb I uninstalled almost every application from it. It took me quite some time to figure out what app is possible to remove and what should be kept to let TV functionality to work. I even had to factory-default it a couple of times because some random apps I removed were crucial for Android to work. :) I think it took me 5-6 hours to clean it. Now it has only basic TV functionality like any dump TV does, I can watch air and cable TV channels, watch movies and play music from USB storage. If there's a need to watch something online, I connect it over HDMI to my small mini-PC that runs FreeBSD. I think I'm satisfied with the result. :-)PS: Yesterday I opened the case and disconnected WiFi antenna. Just in case.

First of all, open the TV and disconnect the wireless radio from the main board, on mine (Samsung) it was just unplugging one cable (AI or Google it). I dislike doing stuff like that, but it was easy in my case, maybe you'll be lucky, too.Second, never use the "apps" built into the TV.Next, don't plug Ethernet into the TV. Plug HDMI cables into the TV.Use a box of your choice on the other end of the HDMI cables. This is now the box that you trust. (Roku? Shield? Blu-ray? MacBook? PC? Linux? Playstation? XBox? Whatever you want.)The Smart TV itself is now fine. Choose the devices you plug into it to play content. The TV just shows it.

- Buy an LG OLED TV. They're as gorgeous as they are notorious. I just got a 77" LG C6 and it is crazy good.- Root it [0].- Install Glasshouse [1] and disable all telemetry. YOU now own the glass. Now you can chromecast to the TV, use Adfree YouTube, access IP TV, etc etc etc. No point crippling your TV by pulling the wireless module and voiding your warranty.- Install a bunch of cool apps to your TV [2] (there are many more out there besides those listed here)- Restore to Factory Defaults if you ever want / need to unroot and get back to stock e.g. a warranty claimThe only issue is that LG recently closed the vulnerability that made rooting possible so you don't want any firmware released after 2026-10-10 like 43.21.84. Hopefully a new exploit is found that makes rooting possible once again.BTW, you might have heard of Dev Mode on these TVs but they don't allow anywhere near the functionality that rooting provides.[0] https://tv.slada.sk/guides/rooting-guide[1] https://github.com/rorygallagher2024/glasshouse[2] https://www.webosbrew.org/

articles.title: Proving and improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
articles.summary: Proving and improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs

top_comments: Different mathematical framework, but I wonder if this could be better understood using sheaf theory: each modality captures part of the same underlying reality, and those different views can be glued into a consistent bigger picture(Very basic intro: https://www.quantamagazine.org/what-are-sheaves-20240719/)

I haven't read this paper in details, but I have read papers about the platonic hypothesis in the past. Usually one of their weakness is about the design an experiment proving that "neural networks converges towards the same latent space when scaling". Usually authors are effectively proving a subset of the hypothesis, that can be explained by the size of the model and the transfer learning part, leaving not definite answer.Here it seems that their definition is more robust (the representation is defined up to a rotation), but I am wondering how much more re-training they need to perform.

I'm not sure how I feel about the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.In some ways it seems like it should be profound, but part of me thinks it might just be saying 'There is an optimal way to perform dimensionality reduction and as things get bigger it is easier to appoximate'
